chunks: Keeping the eye out of the mask. The question: What can you do to ensure the eye stays out of the mask?
Making the eye bigger is one question. Making sure it always passes the mask is another. The answer is to think in budgets. Start from the mask and the error-rate target.
Work out how much time and voltage each impairment is allowed to use. Simulate early, lay out the board to protect the budget, then measure real margin on several boards.
Think of a monthly money budget. Your income is fixed: here it is one bit time. Fixed costs come out first: the room the mask needs.
The rest is spent on jitter, smearing between bits, reflections, crosstalk and supply noise. You want some savings left over at the end.
If the spending exceeds the income, you find out on paper, before building anything.
An illustrative horizontal budget at one unit interval. The impairments consume about half the UI, the mask's keep-out needs 35%, leaving 15% margin.
If any item grows, the margin shrinks first; if margin goes negative the eye touches the mask.
Budget: the share of the bit time and of the voltage swing that each impairment may use.
Mask margin: how much bigger the mask could get before the signal fails ("Eye mask and mask violations").
Guard band: extra margin beyond the minimum, to cover variation from board to board and over time.
Corners: the extreme conditions, such as hot and cold, or high and low supply voltage, where the circuit is checked. Jitter: edges arriving early or late ("Jitter").
A 10 Gb/s link has a bit time of 100 picoseconds.
The jitter sources add up: transmitter 12 picoseconds, channel smearing 22 picoseconds, reflections 6 picoseconds, crosstalk 4 picoseconds, supply and clock circuit 6 picoseconds.
That is 50 picoseconds used. The mask needs 35 picoseconds of clear width. So the budget is 100 - 50 - 35 = 15 picoseconds left over, which is 15% of the bit time.
That 15 picoseconds is the margin to cover variation across boards and temperatures. That is the whole idea: spend the bit time on paper before you build.

"I'd work from the spec to a budget, simulate the channel before layout, protect the budget with controlled impedance, matched lengths, back-drilled vias, spacing and clean supplies, then measure mask margin on real hardware across corners with aggressors running.
I'd aim for comfortable margin, not just a pass, and tune equalization or fix the biggest budget item if margin is thin."
Quick check. What is the best metric to track, beyond simple pass/fail, when keeping an eye out of the mask?
